analysis.one_liner: Repeals the exemption that lets oil and gas fracking escape Safe Drinking Water Act regulation.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was introduced by three House Democrats and died in committee when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Hydraulic fracturing — pumping water, sand, and chemicals underground at high pressure to crack rock and release oil and gas — is currently excluded from the Safe Drinking Water Act's rules for underground injection [S2][S3]. This bill would delete that exclusion, so the EPA could regulate fracking wells the way it regulates other underground injection, with permits and oversight [S2][S3]. The bill was introduced on September 29, 2008, sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee, and never moved again [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink water from wells and aquifers near oil and gas drilling would gain federal protection: fracking operations would need Safe Drinking Water Act permits and would fall under EPA oversight instead of operating outside it [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Safe Drinking Water Act exclusion for hydraulic fracturing, so underground injection of fluids during fracking counts as 'underground injection' under the Act [S3].
Makes fracking wells subject to federal regulation under the Safe Drinking Water Act, which the CRS summary describes as permitting federal regulation of hydraulic fracturing [S2].
Keeps a narrow carve-out for underground storage of natural gas, so storage operations are still excluded [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers and fracking service companies would bear new compliance costs: permits, EPA review, and disclosure of what they inject underground for every fracking operation [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas drillers and fracking firms

drawbacks.text: Fracking operators would face new permitting and compliance costs for each well, which industry argued could slow domestic oil and gas production; the bill contains no cost offset or transition assistance [S3].

The bill gives the EPA authority over fracking under the underground injection program but does not itself fund additional EPA enforcement, so the protection would depend on agency staffing and state implementation [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct and concrete — federal oversight of fluids pumped into the ground near drinking water sources — and the cost is compliance spending by drillers, some of which could be passed to consumers or slow drilling. The bill is a one-page fix that does exactly what its title says and nothing more; it is simple but narrow, and it arrived very late in a Congress that was ending within months.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 2008, referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its environment subcommittee, and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Diana DeGette introduced the bill on September 29, 2008, with Reps. Hinchey and Salazar as original cosponsors [S3].
The same day it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and then to the Subcommittee on Environment and Hazardous Materials [S5].
No further action was taken: the bill received no committee vote and never reached the House floor before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers and fracking service companies are better off, because the industry keeps its exemption from Safe Drinking Water Act permitting and regulation. Households near drilling sites remain without federal Safe Drinking Water Act protection for fracking operations.

for.name: Rep. Diana DeGette
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the fracking exemption from the Safe Drinking Water Act.

against.name: Rep. John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill the day it was introduced and took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.role: Industry holding the exemption the bill would repeal
against.what_they_did: Opposed extending Safe Drinking Water Act permitting to hydraulic fracturing, which the 2005 energy law had exempted from the Act's underground injection rules.

sides.party_line_note: Only three Democrats sponsored the bill, no roll-call vote was ever taken, and the Democratic chairman whose committee held it took no action, so the record shows no clear party split — just inaction.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and fracking service companies
industries.note: Fracking currently escapes the Safe Drinking Water Act's underground injection permitting because of the exemption this bill would repeal. Losing it would mean EPA permits, oversight, and compliance costs for every fracking job — costs the industry's gain from the exemption pushes onto people who drink water near drilling sites.
